newsitem.title: GERMANY: FORECAST - German 1996 GDP growth seen about 1.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - German 1996 GDP growth seen about 1.5 pct.

text.p: German gross domestic product (GDP) data due this week will show the economy expanded 1.4 or 1.5 percent in 1996, but growth virtually ground to a halt in the final quarter, economists said on Tuesday.

In what is threatening to be a repeat performance of last year, cold weather could hamper construction to such an extent that the economy might contract in the first quarter of 1997, with little improvement likely before the spring, they said.
The Federal Statistics Office will release preliminary 1996 GDP data at a news conference on Thursday at 0900 GMT.

The Statistics Office will not announce a figure for final quarter 1996 GDP because it does not yet have enough data but economists expect some indication of how the economy fared during the last three months of 1996.

Most economists polled by Reuters expect the final quarter of 1996 to show quarter-on-quarter growth of about 0.2 percent, a sharp deceleration from one percent growth in the third quarter and 1.5 percent in the second.

The main reason for the slowdown is the general realisation that mass unemployment is hear to stay which, coupled with meagre wage rises agreed for the coming years, will keep consumers as reluctant as ever to open their wallets.
"Companies are incredibly sceptical, they are not convinced Germany has the preconditions for sustained growth," said Holger Fahrinkrug, an economist at UBS in Germany.
"There's a very big question mark over domestic demand and Germany cannot live from exports alone."

Germany's DGB trade union federation sounded further alarm bells on Tuesday, warning that unadjusted December unemployment, due to be released on Thursday, would rise to 4.1 million before hitting a post-war record of between 4.5 and 4.6 million by February.

Analysts noted that the stronger GDP growth seen in the second and third quarters of 1996 was driven by exports and partly exaggerated by economic activity recovering from an extremely weak first quarter when GDP contracted 0.5 percent.
Meanwhile growth is not expected to pick up significantly before the spring of 1997.

"We are seeing a levelling off in the winter months, a pause in growth that will last for two quarters," said Uwe Angenendt, an economist at BHF-Bank. He estimates growth slowed to 0.2 percent in the last quarter.

Angenendt said the economy may even contract in the first three months of 1997 because of the cold weather, the negative impact on consumer spending of a rise in pension contributions this year and a cut in tax breaks for investors in east Germany.
Matthias Haffner, an economist at Barclays de Zoete Wedd in Frankfurt, estimates the economy grew 1.4 percent in 1996 with growth slowing to 0.5 percent at most in the final quarter.
Haffner sees steady growth of 0.5 percent in the first three months of 1997 but said the economy could contract if the present spell of freezing weather lasts another two weeks.
